Hill numbers: taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional diversity

Source: vignettes/hill_diversity.Rmd
hill_diversity.Rmd

MicroBioMeta computes diversity and returns the figure ready for publication. This tutorial explains the Hill-number framework and how to use it in the functions that work with it: alpha_hill_plot() and alpha_diversity_plot() for alpha diversity, and beta_ord_plot() and beta_test_table() for beta diversity. The calculations with a tree or with traits come from hilldiv3 (Alberdi and Gilbert 2019).

Why Hill numbers

Hill numbers (Hill 1973; Jost 2007) express diversity as an effective number: how many equally abundant taxa would give the same diversity as the sample. A sample with a value of 10 is twice as diverse as one with a value of 5, a statement that does not hold for the Shannon or Simpson indices.

The order qq sets how much weight the abundances get:

Order Weight of the taxa Equivalent to
q=0q = 0 All count the same Richness
q=1q = 1 In proportion to their abundance Exponential of Shannon
q=2q = 2 Mostly the dominant ones Inverse of Simpson

The same idea extends to two other dimensions of diversity. Here each one has its own unit, so the values of the three types cannot be compared with each other: compare groups within a type.

diversity What it takes into account What you need Unit
"taxonomic" Abundances The table Effective number of features
"phylogenetic" How related the taxa are (Chao et al. 2010) Rooted tree Effective number of lineages
"functional" How different their traits are (Chao et al. 2019) Traits per taxon Effective number of functionally distinct features

Preparing the data

We use the fungal example of the package (arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, 18S).

library(MicroBioMeta)

table_fungi <- read.delim(
    system.file("extdata", "table_fungi.txt", package = "MicroBioMeta"),
    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE
)
taxonomy_fungi <- read.delim(
    system.file("extdata", "taxonomy_fungi.txt", package = "MicroBioMeta"),
    check.names = FALSE
)
metadata_fungi <- read.delim(
    system.file("extdata", "metadata_fungi.txt", package = "MicroBioMeta"),
    check.names = FALSE
)
metadata_fungi <- metadata_fungi[metadata_fungi$SAMPLEID %in% colnames(table_fungi), ]
table_fungi <- table_fungi[, metadata_fungi$SAMPLEID]

table_fung <- merge_feature_taxonomy(table = table_fungi, taxonomy = taxonomy_fungi)

The tree

The tip labels must be the taxa of the table. With QIIME 2 (Bolyen et al. 2019), the tree comes from the representative sequences, and exported-tree/tree.nwk is what you read in R:

qiime phylogeny align-to-tree-mafft-fasttree \
    --i-sequences rep-seqs.qza \
    --output-dir phylogeny
qiime tools export --input-path phylogeny/rooted_tree.qza --output-path exported-tree
tree_fungi <- ape::read.tree(
    system.file("extdata", "tree_fungi.nwk", package = "MicroBioMeta")
)

Check the tree before you use it: a few spurious sequences on a very long branch can flatten q=1q = 1 and q=2q = 2, because that branch dominates the tree. In this example we removed three Unassigned ASVs (10 reads) for that reason.

The traits

traits is a table with taxa in rows and traits in columns. Any measured trait works. For microbial communities a common source is the table of gene families predicted per ASV by PICRUSt2 (Douglas et al. 2020), such as EC_predicted.tsv. Those are predictions, not measurements, so report them as such.

traits_fungi <- read.delim(
    system.file("extdata", "traits_fungi.txt", package = "MicroBioMeta"),
    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE
)

Taxa that are in the table but not in the tree or the traits are dropped with a warning that says how many. Here that happens with the three ASVs above.

Alpha diversity with Hill numbers

alpha_hill_plot() uses the same call for all three types. Only diversity and its input change, and the y-axis title follows the unit of each type.

alpha_hill_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    facet_by = "Treatment",
    show_legend = FALSE
)

alpha_hill_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    facet_by = "Treatment",
    show_legend = FALSE,
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)

alpha_hill_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    facet_by = "Treatment",
    show_legend = FALSE,
    diversity = "functional",
    traits = traits_fungi,
    stat = "kruskal.test"
)

Two details of these values:

  • The phylogenetic values are read at one common tree depth, so samples are comparable. For that reason a sample can fall slightly below 1.
  • Functional values depend on a distance threshold; here it is the largest distance between two taxa, the default of hilldiv3.

Classic indices

alpha_diversity_plot() shows the classic indices, also with diversity:

diversity Index Meaning Unit
"taxonomic" Chao1, Shannon, Simpson Richness and evenness Different in each index
"phylogenetic" Faith’s PD (Faith 1992) Summed branch length up to the root Branch length
"functional" Rao’s Q (Rao 1982) Mean distance between two random reads Distance (Gower) 
alpha_diversity_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    show_legend = FALSE,
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)

alpha_diversity_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    show_legend = FALSE,
    diversity = "functional",
    traits = traits_fungi
)

These indices are related to the Hill numbers but they are not the same quantity. Faith’s PD is the phylogenetic q=0q = 0 before dividing by the depth of the tree, and Rao’s Q gives the functional q=2q = 2 through 1/(1−Q/τ)1 / (1 - Q / \tau), where τ\tau is the distance threshold. Choose the classic index if you need to compare with studies that report it, and the Hill number if you want every type in the same framework.

Beta diversity

The metrics

hilldiv3::hillpair() turns the Hill numbers into dissimilarities between samples (Jost 2007; Chiu et al. 2014). In MicroBioMeta they are one more option of distance, next to "jaccard" or "aitchison", with the order set by q. They range from 0 (identical samples) to 1 (nothing shared), so they have no unit problem.

distance Type q=0q = 0 q=1q = 1 q=2q = 2
"U" Jaccard type Jaccard Horn Regional overlap
"C" Sørensen type Sørensen Horn Morisita-Horn
"V" Sørensen-type turnover Sørensen
"S" Jaccard-type turnover Jaccard

With diversity = "phylogenetic" and q=0q = 0, "U" is the unweighted UniFrac (Lozupone and Knight 2005). It is a good default if you already use Jaccard. At q=1q = 1 it is related to the weighted UniFrac, but it is not the same value.

These metrics describe the differences in Hill-number terms; they are not compositional. If your main analysis uses CLR/Aitchison, keep it there and use these as a complement.

Ordination

The Hill metrics work with ordination = "PCoA" or "NMDS", the same as any distance that is not "compositional".

beta_ord_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    distance = "U",
    q = 1,
    ordination = "PCoA",
    group_col = "Type_of_soil"
)

beta_ord_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    distance = "U",
    q = 0,
    ordination = "PCoA",
    group_col = "Type_of_soil",
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)

beta_ord_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    distance = "U",
    q = 1,
    ordination = "PCoA",
    group_col = "Type_of_soil",
    diversity = "functional",
    traits = traits_fungi
)

PERMANOVA and betadisper

beta_test_table() takes the same arguments. A PERMANOVA (Anderson 2001) tests whether the groups differ, and betadisper (Anderson 2006) whether their dispersion does. Report both: a significant PERMANOVA with unequal dispersions may reflect differences in dispersion, not in position. In this example betadisper is significant, so read the PERMANOVA of Type_of_soil with that in mind.

beta_test_table(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    formula_str = "Type_of_soil * Treatment",
    distance = "U",
    q = 0,
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)

beta_test_table(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    formula_str = "Type_of_soil",
    distance = "U",
    q = 0,
    test = "betadisper",
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)

References

Alberdi, Antton, and M. Thomas P. Gilbert. 2019. “A Guide to the Application of Hill Numbers to DNA-Based Diversity Analyses.” Molecular Ecology Resources 19 (4): 804–17. https://doi.org/10.1111/1755-0998.13014.
Anderson, Marti J. 2001. “A New Method for Non-Parametric Multivariate Analysis of Variance.” Austral Ecology 26 (1): 32–46. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1442-9993.2001.01070.pp.x.
Anderson, Marti J. 2006. “Distance-Based Tests for Homogeneity of Multivariate Dispersions.” Biometrics 62 (1): 245–53. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2005.00440.x.
Bolyen, Evan, Jai Ram Rideout, Matthew R. Dillon, et al. 2019. “Reproducible, Interactive, Scalable and Extensible Microbiome Data Science Using QIIME 2.” Nature Biotechnology 37 (8): 852–57. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-019-0209-9.
Chao, Anne, Chun-Huo Chiu, and Lou Jost. 2010. “Phylogenetic Diversity Measures Based on Hill Numbers.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 365 (1558): 3599–609. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2010.0272.
Chao, Anne, Chun-Huo Chiu, Sébastien Villéger, et al. 2019. “An Attribute-Diversity Approach to Functional Diversity, Functional Beta Diversity, and Related (Dis)similarity Measures.” Ecological Monographs 89 (2): e01343. https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.1343.
Chiu, Chun-Huo, Lou Jost, and Anne Chao. 2014. “Phylogenetic Beta Diversity, Similarity, and Differentiation Measures Based on Hill Numbers.” Ecological Monographs 84 (1): 21–44. https://doi.org/10.1890/12-0960.1.
Douglas, Gavin M., Vincent J. Maffei, Jesse R. Zaneveld, et al. 2020. “PICRUSt2 for Prediction of Metagenome Functions.” Nature Biotechnology 38 (6): 685–88. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-020-0548-6.
Faith, Daniel P. 1992. “Conservation Evaluation and Phylogenetic Diversity.” Biological Conservation 61 (1): 1–10. https://doi.org/10.1016/0006-3207(92)91201-3.
Hill, M. O. 1973. “Diversity and Evenness: A Unifying Notation and Its Consequences.” Ecology 54 (2): 427–32. https://doi.org/10.2307/1934352.
Jost, Lou. 2007. “Partitioning Diversity into Independent Alpha and Beta Components.” Ecology 88 (10): 2427–39. https://doi.org/10.1890/06-1736.1.
Lozupone, Catherine, and Rob Knight. 2005. “UniFrac: A New Phylogenetic Method for Comparing Microbial Communities.” Applied and Environmental Microbiology 71 (12): 8228–35. https://doi.org/10.1128/AEM.71.12.8228-8235.2005.
Rao, C. Radhakrishna. 1982. “Diversity and Dissimilarity Coefficients: A Unified Approach.” Theoretical Population Biology 21 (1): 24–43. https://doi.org/10.1016/0040-5809(82)90004-1.
